---
title: "Cholesky Decomposition"
description: "An original worked mathematical lesson corresponding to MML §4.3."
---

**Reference:** *Mathematics for Machine Learning*, Chapter 4, §4.3. The teaching example and explanation here are original.

## Why we need this concept

Covariance and normal-equation matrices are often symmetric and positive definite. Cholesky factorisation exploits this structure to solve systems efficiently.

## Derive the structure

$$
A=LL^\top,\qquad \boldsymbol x^\top A\boldsymbol x>0\ \ \forall\boldsymbol x\ne0
$$

Check the shapes and conditions in this statement before applying it. The formula encodes the exact relationship to reason about, rather than replacing a derivation with a library call.

## Worked example

For A=[[4,2],[2,3]], choose lower-triangular L=[[2,0],[1,sqrt(2)]]. Multiplying L L^T gives [[4,2],[2,3]] exactly. A is positive definite because 4>0 and determinant 8>0.

## Interpretation and limitations

The standard Cholesky factor exists uniquely with positive diagonal for symmetric positive-definite matrices. Semidefinite or indefinite matrices require a different treatment or a pivoted/general decomposition.

## Challenge

Why would Cholesky fail for diag(1,-1)? Verify the positivity condition.
